Error Handling, Closures, and Macros

Result: Construct It, Match It

User code can build and return a Result<i32, String> directly, with Ok(...) and Err(...), and handle it with match — the same shape as Rust. The ? operator also works; the second pair below exercises propagation on both sides and was compiled and run.

// Rust
fn divide(a: i32, b: i32) -> Result<i32, String> {
    if b == 0 {
        return Err(String::from("division by zero"));
    }
    Ok(a / b)
}

fn main() {
    match divide(10, 2) {
        Ok(value) => println!("{}", value),
        Err(error) => println!("{}", error),
    }
    match divide(10, 0) {
        Ok(value) => println!("{}", value),
        Err(error) => println!("{}", error),
    }
}
// output: 5, then: division by zero
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn divide(a: i32, b: i32) -> Result<i32, String> {
    if b == 0 {
        return Err(format("division by zero"));
    };
    return Ok(a / b);
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    match divide(10, 2) {
        Ok(value) => { println("{}", value); },
        Err(error) => { println("{}", error); },
    };
    match divide(10, 0) {
        Ok(value) => { println("{}", value); },
        Err(error) => { println("{}", error); },
    };
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 5, then division by zero, exit code 0. The error string is built with format(...), per the first page. Fallible extern functions from the standard library surface errors the same way — as a Result you match with Ok / Err — so library and user errors share one handling style.

Error propagation with ?

Both languages propagate a Result with ?. The Rust version returns Ok(30) then Err("bad number"); the SLA version prints the same two cases in its own format (ok 30, err bad number). Both programs were compiled and run.

// Rust
fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<i32, String> {
    s.parse::<i32>().map_err(|_| String::from("bad number"))
}
fn compute(a: &str, b: &str) -> Result<i32, String> {
    Ok(parse(a)? + parse(b)?)
}
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", compute("10", "20"));
    println!("{:?}", compute("x", "20"));
}
// output: Ok(30) / Err("bad number")
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/core/result.sa"

fn parse(value: i32) -> Result<i32, String> {
    if value < 0 { return Err(format("bad number")); };
    return Ok(value);
}
fn compute(a: i32, b: i32) -> Result<i32, String> {
    let x = parse(a)?;
    let y = parse(b)?;
    return Ok(x + y);
}
fn main() -> i32 {
    match compute(10, 20) {
        Ok(v) => { println("ok {}", v); },
        Err(e) => { println("err {}", e); },
    };
    match compute(-1, 20) {
        Ok(v) => { println("ok {}", v); },
        Err(e) => { println("err {}", e); },
    };
    return 0;
}
// output: ok 30 / err bad number

Option

Option<i32>, Some(7), and None are real and matchable. Both programs below were compiled and run; both print 7 then none.

// Rust
fn find(flag: bool) -> Option<i32> { if flag { Some(7) } else { None } }

fn main() {
    match find(true) { Some(v) => println!("{}", v), None => println!("none") }
    match find(false) { Some(v) => println!("{}", v), None => println!("none") }
}
// output: 7 / none
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn find(flag: bool) -> Option<i32> {
    if flag {
        return Some(7);
    };
    return None;
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    match find(true) {
        Some(v) => { println("{}", v); },
        None => { println("none"); },
    };
    match find(false) {
        Some(v) => { println("{}", v); },
        None => { println("none"); },
    };
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 7, then none, exit code 0.

Closures

Closures use the Rust pipe syntax with typed parameters and capture surrounding bindings:

// Rust
fn main() {
    let factor = 10;
    let multiply = |x: i32| x * factor;
    println!("{}", multiply(5));
}
// output: 50
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let factor = 10;
    let multiply = |x: i32| x * factor;
    println("{}", multiply(5));
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 50, exit code 0. One boundary to know before the concurrency page: a closure that crosses a task boundary may not capture a borrow of an enclosing place — that is checked, and the rejected forms are shown on the &mut comparison page.

Macros: Typed, with a Leading Output Parameter

SLA user macros are not macro_rules!. A macro is typed — its parameters have types and its body is checked like a function body — and its first parameter is the output: the macro writes its result into that parameter, and the call site reads like a function call returning it. Rust's macro_rules! is a different mechanism — pattern-based rather than typed — but the hygiene property is the same: a temp declared inside the macro does not touch the caller's temp. The verified Rust program prints 6 then 5; the SLA program prints 42.

// Rust
macro_rules! add_one { ($v:expr) => {{ let temp = 1; $v + temp }}; }

fn main() {
    let temp = 5;
    println!("{}", add_one!(temp));
    println!("{}", temp);
}
// output: 6 / 5
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

macro doubled(out_result: i64, x: i64) {
    out_result = x + x;
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let v: i64 = 21;
    let a = doubled(v);
    println("{}", a);
    if a != 42 { return 1; };
    return 0;
}

Verified output: 42, exit code 0. Read the definition as: “doubled takes an i64 input x and produces its result through the leading output parameter out_result.” The call let a = doubled(v); binds that output. For the wider macro comparison — @derive, @overload, and how this differs from Rust's pattern macros — see Macros and Metaprogramming Compared.

Key Points of This Page

  • Result and Option are constructed and matched exactly as a Rust programmer expects; error strings are built with format(...).
  • Closures use |x: i32| expr syntax and capture enclosing bindings; borrows still may not cross task boundaries.
  • SLA user macros are typed, checked like functions, and take a leading output parameter; the call site looks like a function call.
